title: MB3-00553
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, the claimant, is a citizen of Turkey and is basing his claim on sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The panel determines that the claimant is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.
The claimant fears the Turkish nationalists and police by reason of his Kurdish ethnic origin and his Alevi religion.

The claimant stated in his Basis of Claim Form that the events of 1978 in XXXX affected his entire family. His uncle was very politically active at that time, and his father changed his name XXXX Topal to XXXX because of the problems.
During the Newroz celebration in 2007, the claimant was arrested in XXXX, detained, threatened, and released the next day.

In XXXX 2009, the claimant was arrested again when he took part in a rally for the Democratic Society Party (DTP), which is now the Peace and Democracy Party (BDP). He was beaten during his one-day detention.
In XXXX 2011 (during the XXXX XXXX XXXX), he was attacked by a group of Islamists during a gathering in XXXX at a Cem house for "Ashure." The police did nothing and did not take their complaints.
On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012, during the commemoration of the Sivas massacre in 1993, he was caught in a confrontation with the police. He was arrested, threatened and beaten. ANALYSIS Identity
The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity. His identity was established by the copy of his passport and national identity card (Exhibit A-2) and by his testimony. Credibility

The panel has doubts about the claimant's credibility with regard to his Alevi and Kurdish identity. The claimant gave vague testimony that lacked details and that was filled with generalities with respect to his allegations concerning his Kurdish ethnicity and Alevi religion, aspects at the root of his refugee protection claim.
Nevertheless, the panel gives the claimant the benefit of the doubt with respect to his allegations concerning his Kurdish ethnicity and Alevi religion.

Concerning his allegations regarding his arrests by the police during demonstrations, the claimant alleged that he fears the police and nationalists. He described three different events during which he was allegedly arrested. These arrests allegedly took place during demonstrations or rallies. The first incident took place on March 21, 2007, during the Newroz celebration. The police allegedly arrested a group of ten people. When the panel asked him about what he was doing during the celebration or about what was happening, the claimant was unable to provide detailed information. His answers were vague, and he hesitated tremendously before answering. The panel notes certain issues regarding his credibility, but also gives him the benefit of the doubt. Documentary evidence Alevi The documentary evidence on the situation of Alevis indicates that the Turkish government generally allows religions to be practised freely, as stated in document 2.21 of the National Documentation Package on Turkey: 18.15 Though not granted status as a religious minority, Alevis reportedly are able to practice their beliefs relatively freely. Nevertheless, the Alevis are still subject to some discriminatory state practices, though their situation has improved in recent years. and 8.18 During the year police routinely detained demonstrators for a few hours at a time. Police detained several hundred members of the former DTP [Democratic Society Party] and its successor Peace and Democracy Party (BDP) on various occasions. Police continued to detain and harass members of human rights organizations, media personnel, and human rights monitors. Police continued to detain persons on suspicion of 'membership in an illegal organization' and for 'promoting terrorist propaganda'. Kurd

Kurds are the largest ethnic minority in Turkey. The evidence shows that Kurds who publicly or politically assert their Kurdish identity or promote using Kurdish in the public domain risk censure, harassment, or prosecution (2.1).2 That document also states as follows: The government harassed and prosecuted persons sympathetic to some religious, political, and Kurdish nationalist or cultural viewpoints. ... Other significant human rights problems during the year included: Security forces committed unlawful killings. Authorities obstructed demonstrations. Security forces allegedly used excessive force during sometimes violent protests related to the Kurdish issue, students' rights, and labor and opposition activities. The government obstructed the activities of human rights organizations, particularly in the Southeast."

Document 2.23 states as follows: 14.13 The USSD Report 2009, also observed that: "The HRF [Human Rights Foundation] reported that security forces killed seven persons during demonstrations and injured 269, and there were reports that police beat, abused, detained, or harassed some demonstrators during the year. The HRF reported that security forces detained 1,414 persons and arrested and charged 369 during demonstrations during the year ...The approximately 180 public events around the country celebrating the Nevruz holiday (the Kurdish and Persian New Year) in March were generally peaceful. The HRF reported no incidents during Nevruz celebrations in the year, compared to numerous deaths and injuries during the previous year." 14.14 The EC Progress Report 2009, observed that: "Newroz (the Kurdish New Year) and 1 May [2009] demonstrations, which were marred by police violence in previous years, took place peacefully in most places during the reporting period. However, demonstrations in the South-East of the country continued to be marked by violence. Investigation and videotaping of NGOs' activities by security forces are still being reported, especially in the East and South-East of the country."

In addition, the Country Reports on Human Rights Practices for 2012 states approximately the same facts, but indicates that some of these celebrations were banned or postponed for arbitrary reasons and that violence was noted in Diyarkir, a city in southeast Turkey. The government limited celebrations of the Kurdish holiday Newroz (New Year) to March 21, and the HRA reported that the Ministry of Interior banned or postponed 129 planned Newroz celebrations for arbitrary reasons. Clashes broke out, particularly in Diyarbakir, and police used gas bombs and water cannons against the crowd. According to the HRA, two persons were killed, 178 wounded, 1,014 detained, and 206 arrested during the celebrations. Haci Zengin, a BDP branch office head in Istanbul, died after being hit on the head by a tear gas canister.4 Prospective fear

After assessing all the documentary evidence, the panel is not satisfied that Alevi Kurds are persecuted in general, but they appear to be the victims of discrimination and in some cases persecution. Regarding the claimant, his testimony and the evidence do not indicate that he has a well-founded prospective fear of persecution. The panel does not believe that the claimant would be persecuted if he returned to Turkey.

This finding is supported by the behaviour of the police toward the claimant during his arrests and after his detentions. On the one hand, the evidence shows that the claimant was arrested at random during demonstrations without investigations by the police officers into his identity. On the other hand, the police never pursued the claimant. He was released after each detention, he managed to obtain a passport, and he was able to leave Turkey.

The claimant also does not fit the profile of a political or Kurdish activist and is not a member of any political party. He was arrested when he participated in various demonstrations that were unrelated. The first demonstration was for a Kurdish holiday. The second was related to a political rally for the DTP. The third was for the commemoration of the Sivas massacre (an Alevi massacre in 1993). The final event took place during a confrontation with an Islamist group in a Cem house. Moreover, the documentary evidence shows that it is mostly Kurds who have a public and political profile who are harassed, pursued or targeted by the police, and that is not the case for the claimant (document 2.1).5 That documentary evidence does not indicate that violent demonstrations for Newroz took place in XXXX, the claimant's city of residence, in 2012. Document 2.26 indicates that violence during these events decreased in 2009.

In addition, the claimant did not allege that he experienced employment issues. He held a job as a XXXX in Turkey until 2013. He managed to attend secondary school and raised no issues concerning his right to an education. He also did not allege that he had issues with housing. He lived in the same location in Turkey from XXXX 2003 until he left for Canada.

The panel does not believe that the claimant would be subjected to a reasonable fear of persecution by reason of his actual or imputed political opinion, ethnicity or religion if he returned to Turkey. The claimant failed to establish that he would be persecuted for these reasons, given the randomness of the incidents experienced, the lack of a profile that could relate him to the possible incidents of persecution indicated by the objective evidence, and the development of the situation with respect to Newroz demonstrations in recent years.
Given the foregoing, the panel determines that the claimant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution and is therefore not a "Convention refugee."

In addition, since the claimant failed to establish a mere possibility of persecution, he also failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that he would be subjected to a risk to his life, to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment and to torture.
For all these reasons, the panel determines that the claimant is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection."

The refugee protection claim is rejected.
